rows.title: Polynomial quantum Schur first levels: Weyl filtration and the actual Hecke corner
rows.statement:
Put $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$, $q=v^2$, and use the actual integral tensor action and the finite normalized-cell constructions of [[lem-integral-divided-power-tensor-action-surjects-onto-type-a-q-schur-algebra]] and [[lem-integral-quantum-highest-weight-modules-identify-with-normalized-q-schur-weyl-cells]]. For $N>d\ge1$, $\lambda\vdash d$, and $W_N(\lambda)$ its Weyl module, the **first level** is $W_N(\lambda)^1=\bigoplus_{\alpha_N=1}W_N(\lambda)_\alpha$. It has an integral lower-Schur Weyl filtration with one factor $W_{N-1}(\lambda(i))$ for each removable row $i$, ordered by decreasing dominance of $\lambda(i)$. This filtration and its quotient identifications commute with arbitrary coefficient-ring base change.

Over every field with a chosen unit $v$, write $\nabla=W^\tau$ and $L=W/\operatorname{rad}B_\tau$, with the suppliers' abstract highest norm-one form. Then $\operatorname{Hom}(W_{N-1}(\mu),\nabla_N(\lambda)^1)$ is one dimensional exactly for $\mu=\lambda(i)$, and zero otherwise. The same Hom-space with target $L_N(\lambda)^1$ has dimension at most one and vanishes off these labels. Equivalently every lower-Levi primitive line of $L_N(\lambda)^1$ has one of these weights, with dimension at most one; primitive means annihilated by **all** positive divided generators.

For every commutative ring $R$, unit $q$, and left $S_R(N,d)$-module $V$, its first level carries the actual lower algebra $S_R(N-1,d-1)$ action induced on permutation modules, and there is a natural isomorphism
$$e_{\rm lower}V^1\cong\operatorname{Res}^{H_d}_{H_{d-1}}eV.$$
The quantum Levi action, when a square root is chosen, agrees with this action under the actual tensor identification and the suppliers' weight-unit conjugation. This statement neither equates first level with a simple-root layer nor asserts that an exact corner functor preserves socles.
rows.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The rings, ranks, actual permutation-module Schur algebras, weight projections, and normalized Weyl modules of the Statement.

[F1] The actual integral divided tensor action surjects onto $S$, its weight blocks identify tensor space with the permutation-summand realization, and this survives arbitrary base change ([[lem-integral-divided-power-tensor-action-surjects-onto-type-a-q-schur-algebra]]).

[F2] The finite cellular construction and weight-unit transport are the explicit arguments in the cellular-highest-induction, polynomial-universality and direct-cell-form paragraphs of [[lem-integral-quantum-highest-weight-modules-identify-with-normalized-q-schur-weyl-cells]]. The integral highest-lattice quotient and its global-basis isomorphism are not used. Step 1.1 below proves the exact needed cell interfaces without their inherited Choice.

[F3] The Weyl cell is free with the actual semistandard-tableau basis, weight ranks are its tableau counts, and all weights are dominated by $\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Permuting composition contents preserves their tableau counts by the finite bijections of [[lem-bender-knuth-involutions-on-semistandard-tableaux]]. The divided-power reordering establishes triangular spanning integrally; it does not require the freeness or full PBW-rank theorem ([[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]]).

## Proof

1.1 Establish the finite cell interfaces directly. Give the actual right Weyl cell the left action $u\cdot w=w\rho(\tau(u))$. Its canonical vector $h$ is highest: the semistandard weight bounds exclude $\lambda+a\alpha_i$, and its toral character is $\lambda$; the canonical cell form has $B_{\rm cell}(h,h)=1$. The cell law gives $h\varphi_{T^\lambda T}=w_T$, and [F1]'s integral surjection makes it cyclic highest. For a polynomial cyclic highest module $X=U^-x$ of weight $\lambda$, triangular spanning gives weights in $\lambda-Q_+$, so every partition projection $1_\eta$ with $\eta>\lambda$ annihilates it. The higher cellular ideal is generated by these projections: in decreasing shape order $\varphi_{S,T^\eta}1_\eta\varphi_{T^\eta,T}\equiv\varphi_{ST}$ modulo higher shapes, with coefficient one. Hence that ideal kills $X$. Thus $S1_\lambda\to X$, $s1_\lambda\mapsto sx$, factors through the actual left Weyl cell $S1_\lambda/I^{>\lambda}1_\lambda$; its basis is exactly the shape-$\lambda$ columns because semistandard type $\lambda$ requires shape at least $\lambda$. The unit diagonal $C=\sum_\mu c_\mu1_\mu$, $c_\mu=v^{-\sum_j\binom{\mu_j}{2}}$, of [F1] transports this left-star cell to the displayed left quantum action, giving its universal highest property. On its actual weight-$\mu$ vectors define $B=(c_\lambda/c_\mu)B_{\rm cell}$ and different-weight pairings zero. The exact identity $\rho(\tau(u))=C^{-1}\rho(u)^*C$ makes this symmetric integral form $\tau$-contravariant: the right-action weight factor $c_\nu/c_\mu$ is canceled by $(c_\lambda/c_\nu)(c_\nu/c_\mu)=c_\lambda/c_\mu$. Its highest value is one. All factors are units, so its radical is precisely the actual cell radical and its simple quotient is self-dual. These are finite cellular and matrix arguments, valid after arbitrary base change and with no use of the free global highest lattice. [F1, F2, F3, algebra, construct]

1.2 Construct the corner over the original $R,q$. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(N-1,d-1)}m_\alpha H_{d-1}$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases identify $M_1=\bigoplus_\alpha m_{(\alpha,1)}H_d$ with $M_0\otimes_{H_{d-1}}H_d$, by $m_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto m_\alpha ha$. Hence $f\mapsto f\otimes1$, extended by zero on the other summands, embeds the lower Schur algebra with identity $p=\sum_{\alpha_N=1}1_\alpha$. It is injective because the unit parabolic coset supplies a direct summand. The lower regular composition induces the upper regular type $\omega_*=(1^{d-1},0^{N-d},1)$, so $e_{\rm lower}pV=e_*V$. On that summand the lower Hecke corner acts by left multiplication by exactly $h\in H_{d-1}$ on $H_d$, since $h\otimes a\mapsto ha$. [given, F3, algebra, construct]

2.1 Use the root convention $F_{i,i+1}=F_i$ and $F_{i,j}=vF_{i+1,j}F_i-F_iF_{i+1,j}$. In the negative algebra, its last-simple-root-degree-one part is spanned by $xF_{i,N}$ with $x$ in the negative lower Levi. Here is a direct spanning proof, requiring no specialized PBW independence. Every divided-simple-generator word of this degree has exactly one $F_{N-1}$, exponent one; all other generators belong to the lower Levi. Move each factor to its right past the current root using $$F_{i,N}F_{i-1}^{(s)}=v^{-s}F_{i-1}^{(s)}F_{i,N}+v^{-1}F_{i-1}^{(s-1)}F_{i-1,N},\qquad F_{i,N}F_i^{(s)}=v^sF_i^{(s)}F_{i,N}.$$ Other lower simple divided generators commute with $F_{i,N}$. The first identity follows from $vF_{i,N}F_{i-1}=F_{i-1}F_{i,N}+F_{i-1,N}$ and $F_{i-1,N}F_{i-1}=vF_{i-1}F_{i-1,N}$: induction on ordinary powers gives coefficient $v^{-1}[s]$, canceled with $[s]!$ in the generic algebra, leaving the displayed integral identity. The second and remaining commutations follow by inserting the root recurrence into the rank-two Serre identity and then inducting on the interval length; the only noncommuting lower adjacent endpoint is $i-1$, already treated. Each move removes one right factor, so it terminates. Triangular spanning and the highest-vector relations now show $W^1=\sum_iU^-_{N-1}F_{i,N}z_\lambda$. If $\lambda_i=\lambda_{i+1}$, the weight $\lambda-\epsilon_i+\epsilon_{i+1}$ is absent: its sorted weight strictly dominates $\lambda$, contrary to the tableau support. Thus $F_i z_\lambda=0$ and the root recurrence gives $F_{i,N}z_\lambda=-F_iF_{i+1,N}z_\lambda$. Iteration removes all nonremovable rows. Rows beyond the height contribute zero by nonnegative weight support. Therefore the claimed removable-row generators span integrally. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Order these rows as $i_1>\cdots>i_t$, so $\mu_j=\lambda(i_j)$ decreases in dominance, and let $W_j$ be the negative lower-Levi span of the first $j$ generators, with $W_0=0$. Inductively suppose $W_{j-1}$ is invariant. In $W^1/W_{j-1}$ every weight lies below a remaining generator weight by step 2.1, and $\mu_j$ is their maximum. Every positive divided generator kills the image of $F_{i_j,N}z_\lambda$, since its target weight is strictly above $\mu_j$. Triangular spanning makes its negative span invariant. The actual universal highest property gives a surjection $W_{N-1}(\mu_j)\to W_j/W_{j-1}$. This proves invariance and these integral surjections at each stage, without dividing a quantum integer. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Exactly one entry $N$ in a semistandard $\lambda$-tableau lies at a removable corner, and deleting it gives a semistandard $\lambda(i)$-tableau on $1,\ldots,N-1$. Conversely appending $N$ at that corner preserves semistandardness. Consequently the actual free ranks satisfy $\operatorname{rank}W^1=\sum_j\operatorname{rank}W_{N-1}(\mu_j)$. Over $\mathbb Q(v)$ the surjections of step 3.1 and this dimension equality force equality of every quotient dimension. The kernel of each integral surjection lies in the free $A$-module $W_{N-1}(\mu_j)$ and has generic rank zero; injectivity into its fraction-field extension therefore makes that kernel zero. Each integral quotient is thus the actual free lower Weyl module. Its freeness makes the successive short exact sequences split as $A$-module sequences, so arbitrary base change preserves the filtration injections, quotients and surjections. Generic dimensions were used only to prove kernels of explicit integral surjections vanish, not to replace a specialized construction. [F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Over a field let $B^-$ denote the actual lower Borel image. A $B^-$-map $W^1\to F_\mu$ is determined by its values at the generators of step 2.1; their weights are distinct, so its dimension is at most one and is zero off $\mu_j$. At $\mu_j$, quotient by $W_{j-1}$. This quotient has no weight above $\mu_j$, its $\mu_j$-space is the one-dimensional generator line by step 4.1, and later generator weights lie strictly below it. Taking that generator's coefficient, and zero on every other weight, is a well-defined nonzero $B^-$-map, since a nonconstant negative operator cannot reach $\mu_j$. This proves dimension exactly one. The universal highest property gives $\operatorname{Hom}(W_{N-1}(\mu),X)=\operatorname{Hom}_{B^+}(F_\mu,X)$ for every polynomial $X$: maps are exactly primitive vectors of that weight. Taking contravariant duals identifies this with $\operatorname{Hom}_{B^-}(X^\tau,F_\mu)$. With $X=(W^1)^\tau$ this proves the first Hom assertion. With $X=L^1$, self-duality and the injection $L^1\hookrightarrow(W^1)^\tau$ give the upper bound and label restriction. For a primitive vector $x$ of any composition weight, the functional $y\mapsto B(x,y)$ on $L^1$, pulled back to $W^1$, is nonzero by the nondegenerate homogeneous form and kills every nonconstant negative lower operator by contravariance. Thus it is a $B^-$-map to the character of that weight. The same generator bound excludes all other primitive weights, without presupposing their dominance. The form's toral weight orthogonality ensures first-level projection commutes with this duality. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Record the precise coefficient test needed by lowering arguments. If $L^1\to\nabla_{N-1}(\lambda(i))$ is nonzero, compose with $W^1\to L^1$ and with the highest-weight coefficient in $\nabla$. The resulting $B^-$-functional is nonzero, hence nonzero at $F_{i,N}z_\lambda$ by step 5.1. Every nonempty cut product $F_{i,b_1}F_{b_1,b_2}\cdots F_{b_s,N}z_\lambda$ has a nonconstant lower-Levi factor to the left and is killed by this functional. Multiplying factors by the unit toral normalization used for $\widehat F$ changes only their nonzero scalar factors on these fixed weight vectors. Thus the same zero/nonzero test applies to the normalized cut products. This argument needs neither an inherited tensor norm nor a claimed full-Hom surjection at singular parameters. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The summands of types $\omega_*=(1^{d-1},0^{N-d},1)$ and $\omega=(1^d,0^{N-d})$ are both the actual regular module $H_d$. Their identity isomorphisms give block matrix units $u,v$ in $S$ with $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Multiplication by $u$ and $v$ consequently identifies $eV$ with $e_*V$, transporting every lower Hecke operator to its actual upper corner inclusion. This proves the natural restriction isomorphism, including $d=1$, whose lower algebra and corner are $R$. In the tensor realization of [F1], on words containing exactly one $N$ every lower divided generator leaves that position untouched and applies its subset-sum formula to the remaining ordered positions. These are exactly the induced operators of step 1.2 under the actual tensor/permutation intertwiner. Weight projections agree as well, so [F1]'s lower surjectivity proves equality of the full lower actions. The weight-unit diagonal conjugation of [F2] restricts to this subspace and intertwines the same actions after left/right conversion. This verifies the quantum/cellular comparison at every specialization by explicit generators. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

references.title: Jonathan Brundan, Modular branching rules and the Mullineux map for Hecke algebras of type A, §§3.17–3.22 and 5.5–5.6

rows.title: General Hecke residue branching endpoints from normalized Schur cells
rows.statement:
Let $F$ be any field, $q\in F^\times$ have finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, and let $H_d=H_{F,q}(S_d)$ with $(T_j-q)(T_j+1)=0$. Use the actual Murphy cell-form quotients $D(\lambda)$, indexed by $e$-restricted partitions, converted to left modules by star. For additive Hecke JM elements $L_d$, let $E_i$ be the $[i]_q$-generalized eigenspace in restriction to $H_{d-1}$; let $F_i$ be induction followed by its commuting right $[i]_q$-primary projector. These functors are defined over $F$, for $i\in\mathbb Z/e$, with $[i]_1=i$ and $[i]_q=(q^i-1)/(q-1)$ otherwise.

For every restricted $\lambda$ the nonzero $E_iD(\lambda)$ have simple socle and simple head $D(\widetilde e_i\lambda)$, each once, and $E_iD(\lambda)=0$ exactly when the good $i$-deletion is undefined. Similarly the nonzero $F_iD(\mu)$ have simple socle and simple head $D(\widetilde f_i\mu)$, each once, and vanish exactly when the cogood $i$-addition is undefined. Here signatures use content $c-r$, top-to-bottom order, cancellation of $-+$, first surviving minus and last surviving plus ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). In particular the restriction socle is the multiplicity-free sum over good residues. This proves endpoints, not total composition multiplicities. Composite $e$, arbitrary characteristic, nonsquare $q$, and rank zero are included.
rows.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, actual cellular labels, residue convention and functors of the Statement.

[F1] The first-level Weyl filtration, one-dimensional primitive/Hom bound and coefficient test, and the actual integral permutation/tensor corner identification are proved in [[lem-polynomial-quantum-schur-first-level-weyl-filtration-and-hecke-corner]]. That supplier constructs the abstract highest norm-one form directly on the actual finite cell; it has radical the maximal submodule and gives self-dual simples. Its complete local finite-cell construction is used; no Choice-bearing free global highest-lattice isomorphism is invoked.

[F2] Central symmetric JM operators act on actual Schur Weyl cells by their node-content scalars, and every constituent retains their full residue multiset ([[lem-q-schur-central-hecke-jm-scalars-give-residue-separation]]).

[F3] The actual corner and restricted-label classifier identifies the surviving Schur simple with the actual same-label Murphy simple; these are complete, distinct and absolutely simple over the original field ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]). The standard trace is symmetric and satisfies $\tau(T_u^*T_w)=\delta_{u,w}q^{\ell(w)}$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Additive JM elements commute, centralize the preceding algebra, are star-fixed, and have triangular q-content spectra ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

[F4] At $q=1$, the actual group restriction endpoint is supplied by the initial restriction construction (the first seventeen phases) of [[thm-cogood-node-gives-the-simple-socle-and-head-of-residue-induction]], independently of its final composition-multiplicity argument. Its actual restricted-label convention is retained. No inverse of $q-1$ is specialized to zero.

## Proof

1.1 First construct the coefficient polynomials without specializing denominators. For $i<j$, $I=(i,j)$, $D\subseteq I$ and $p_D(t)=\max(\{i\}\cup\{d\in D:d<t\})$, define $$H(A,B)=\sum_{D\subseteq B\setminus A}(-1)^{|D|}\frac{\prod_{t\in A}(x_t-x_{p_D(t)})}{\prod_{t\in B}(x_t-x_{p_D(t)})}.$$ Cancel common $A\cap B$. For disjoint sets let $h=\min(A\cup B)$. If $h\in A$, multiply $H(A\setminus\{h\},B)$ by $x_h-x_i$. If $h\in B$, put $P=H(A,B\setminus\{h\})$; splitting the sum according to $h\in D$ gives $(P-P|_{x_i=x_h})/(x_h-x_i)$. Divided difference of $x_i^m$ is $-\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}x_i^ax_h^{m-1-a}$, so induction proves $H\in\mathbb Z[x]$ even at coincident coordinates. Also $H(\varnothing,B)=\delta_{B,\varnothing}$ by the same recursion. For $k\in A$, $h=\max([i,k)\setminus A)$, splitting $x_k-x_{p_D(k)}=(x_k-x_h)+(x_h-x_{p_D(k)})$ gives $$H(A,B)=(x_k-x_h)H(A\setminus\{k\},B)+\mathbf1_{h\ne i}H((A\setminus\{k\})\cup\{h\},B)+\mathbf1_{k\in B}H_{i,k}(A\cap(i,k),B\cap(i,k))H_{k,j}(A\cap(k,j),B\cap(k,j)).$$ Indeed $(h,k)\subseteq A$, so common factors there first cancel. The second difference is zero when $h\in D$; otherwise its predecessor equals $p_D(h)$, giving the second term. The extra $k\in D$ terms have negative sign and split independently at $k$, giving the positive third product after subtraction. This accounts for every summand. [given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Put $C=I\setminus A$ and $$K(A)=\sum_{B\subseteq I}H(A,B)\prod_{t\in\{i\}\cup B}(y_{t+1}-x_t).$$ Expansion of each $y_{t+1}-x_{p_D(t+1)}$ as $(y_{t+1}-x_t)+(x_t-x_{p_D(t+1)})$ gives $$K(A)=\sum_{D\subseteq C}(-1)^{|D|}\frac{\prod_{t=i}^{j-1}(y_{t+1}-x_{p_D(t+1)})}{\prod_{t\in C}(x_t-x_{p_D(t)})}.$$ Selected difference factors vanish when their index belongs to $D$; the remaining predecessor is $p_D(t)$, and collection gives exactly $H(A,B)$ by cancellation of the complement numerator/denominator sets. For a bijection $\theta:C\to B_0\subseteq I$ with $\theta(c)\ge c$, this implies the matched-product identity $$K(A)\equiv\prod_{t\in[i,j)\setminus B_0}(y_{t+1}-x_i)\pmod{(y_{\theta(c)+1}-x_c:c\in C)}.$$ Here is an integral induction proof. If $C=\varnothing$, the alternating expression is the asserted full product. Otherwise take $h=\min C$, remove its source and target, and apply induction on $(h,j)$. Splitting the alternating sum by $h\in D$ gives the prefix product times the divided difference of $K_{h,j}$ in $x_h$. The prefix is $\prod_{t=i}^{h-1}(y_{t+1}-x_i)$ and the divided difference is $(K_{h,j}|_{x_h=x_i}-K_{h,j})/(x_h-x_i)$. All remaining match generators are independent of $x_h$, so divided differencing retains their ideal. The induction product contains the target $\theta(h)$; modulo its match it vanishes before substitution, and after substitution its factor is $x_h-x_i$. Cancel that integral factor to leave exactly the tail product with this target removed. No target occurs below $h$, since targets are at least their sources. The prefix completes the stated product. All divisions here are polynomial divided differences, not evaluation of rational functions. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $q\ne1$ and temporarily extend $F$ to a field $K$ containing $v$ with $v^2=q$. Take $N>d$, $W=W_N(\lambda)$, $L=W/\operatorname{rad}B_\tau$, and $z=z_\lambda$. Use the actual normalized root operators $$\widehat F_{i,j}=v^{-j}K_jF_{i,j}K_iv^{-i},\quad c_{i,j}=\frac{v^{-2i-1}K_i^2-v^{-2j-1}K_j^2}{v-v^{-1}},\quad b_{i,j}=\frac{v^{-2i-1}K_i^2-v^{-2j-1}K_{j+1}^2}{v-v^{-1}}.$$ The denominator is a field unit since $q\ne1$. Define $S_{i,j}(A)=\sum_{B\subseteq(i,j)}\widehat F_{i,b_1}\cdots\widehat F_{b_s,j}H(A,B)$, evaluating $x_k=-v^{-2k-1}K_k^2/(v-v^{-1})$; use $S_{i,i}=1$. The recurrence of step 1.1 gives $$S_{i,j}(A)=S_{i,j}(A\setminus\{k\})c_{h,k}+\mathbf1_{h\ne i}S_{i,j}((A\setminus\{k\})\cup\{h\})+S_{i,k}(A\cap(i,k))S_{k,j}(A\cap(k,j)).$$ Left-interval toral coefficients commute with right-interval lower roots, so the product order is exactly as displayed. The empty-set operator is $\widehat F_{i,j}$. Rank-one commutation and the root recurrence give $E_i\widehat F_{i,i+1}=\widehat F_{i,i+1}E_i+vb_{i,i}$, $E_i\widehat F_{i,j}=v^{-1}\widehat F_{i,j}E_i-v\widehat F_{i+1,j}$ if $j>i+1$, and $E_{j-1}\widehat F_{i,j}=v\widehat F_{i,j}E_{j-1}+\widehat F_{i,j-1}$ if $i<j-1$. Disjoint indices commute; adjacent exterior indices contribute precisely their $K$-weight factors. These follow by induction inserting $F_{i,j}=vF_{i+1,j}F_i-F_iF_{i+1,j}$ into the simple defining commutators. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Modulo the left ideal $UE_l$, the recurrence gives this complete table: $E_lS_{i,j}(A)=0$ if $l+1\in A$, or $l\notin\{i\}\cup A$ and $l+1\notin A\cup\{j\}$; it is $-vS_{i,l}(A\cap(i,l))S_{l+1,j}(A\cap(l+1,j))$ if $l\in\{i\}\cup A$, $l+1\notin A\cup\{j\}$; it is $S_{i,j-1}(A)$ if $l=j-1\notin\{i\}\cup A$; finally for $j-1\in A$, $h=\max([i,j-1)\setminus A)$ it is $S_{i,j-1}(A\setminus\{j-1\})b_{h,j-1}+\mathbf1_{h\ne i}S_{i,j-1}((A\setminus\{j-1\})\cup\{h\})$. To verify the table induct on $\sum_{a\in A}a$ using step 2.2. Empty $A$ is the elementary table. For $A=\{l+1\}$, $l>i$, expand again at $l$; the two cut remainders are $\widehat F_{i,l}\widehat F_{l+1,j}$ and its negative and cancel. At $l=i$ the cancellation is $b_{i,i}\widehat F_{i+1,j}=\widehat F_{i+1,j}c_{i,i+1}$. For any other $k\in A$ the recurrence splits into intervals, the remote factor commutes, and the other factor uses induction. For the split row reduce to $l=i$ by expanding at $k=l$; if the replacement is $i+1$ its remainder is the vanishing row, and otherwise all terms combine into the recurrence for $S_{i+1,j}$. The shortened-endpoint row uses the same induction at the other end. Expanding at $k=j-1$ gives the final row: $E_{j-1}\widehat F_{j-1,j}$ contributes $vb_{j-1,j-1}$, its weight factor is $v^{-1}$, and $c_{h,j-1}+b_{j-1,j-1}=b_{h,j-1}$. These exhaust all positions. Successive commutation through a cut product gives $E_i\cdots E_{j-1}\widehat F^Bz=v\prod_{t\in\{i\}\cup B}b_{t,t}(\lambda)z$. Summing proves $E_i\cdots E_{j-1}S_{i,j}(A)z=vK(A)(\lambda)z$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Evaluate $b_{i,k}(\lambda)=(q^{\lambda_i-i}-q^{\lambda_{k+1}-k})/(q-1)$ and $c_{i,k}(\lambda)=(q^{\lambda_i-i}-q^{\lambda_k-k})/(q-1)$. Let $B_{i,j}$ be the zero-$b$ set in $[i,j)$ and $C_{i,j}$ the zero-$c$ set in $(i,j)$. Their vanishing is exactly the corresponding equal-residue comparison. If $c_{i,k+1}=0$, then $b_{i,k}\ne0$, because $c_{i,k+1}-b_{i,k}=q^{\lambda_{k+1}-k-1}$ is a unit. Write $B\downarrow C$ for an injection of demands $B$ into supports $C$, sending each demand to a weakly smaller support. For $C\subseteq C_{i,j}$, we claim nonzero $S_{i,j}((i,j)\setminus C)z$ in $L$ implies $B_{i,j}\downarrow C$. Induct on $j-i$. At length one the elementary commutator and positive detection give equivalence with $b_{i,i}\ne0$. At larger length some $E_l$ has nonzero image: otherwise all positive divided powers kill this vector, since its deficit has each simple-root coefficient zero or one, so powers greater than one have absent target weights; triangular spanning would generate a proper second highest submodule of the simple $L$. Use the table of step 3.1. In the split case its disjoint factors commute, so both their vectors are nonzero; induction gives matchings on both intervals, and $c_{i,l+1}=0$, $b_{i,l}\ne0$ identify the split demands with the full ones. If $j-1\in C$, induction on the shortened interval matches old demands and the extra demand, when present, uses $j-1$. Otherwise put $h=\max(\{i\}\cup C)$ in the last table row. A nonzero first term has $b_{h,j-1}=b_{i,j-1}\ne0$, so there is no new demand. A nonzero second term matches old demands into $C\setminus\{h\}$; the released largest support $h$ handles the only possible new demand $j-1$. This proves the claim in every case. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 A primitive line of $L^1$ at $\lambda(i)$ exists exactly when $B_{i,N}\downarrow C_{i,N}$. For necessity, dualize a nonzero primitive map using [F1] to get $L^1\to\nabla(\lambda(i))$. Its highest coefficient functional on $W^1$ is nonzero at $\widehat F_{i,N}z$ and zero at all nonempty cut products, by [F1]'s exact coefficient test. On $S_{i,N}(A)z$, $A=(i,N)\setminus C_{i,N}$, its value is therefore that nonzero value times $H(A,\varnothing)(\lambda)=\prod_{t\in A}c_{i,t}(\lambda)\ne0$. This vector survives the radical, so step 4.1 gives necessity. Conversely choose a matching with image $C\subseteq C_{i,N}$ of size $|B_{i,N}|$ and invert it to a bijection $C\to B_{i,N}$ with targets at least their sources. The polynomial match generators in step 2.1 vanish, so $K((i,N)\setminus C)(\lambda)=\prod_{t\in[i,N)\setminus B_{i,N}}b_{i,t}(\lambda)\ne0$. Step 3.1 makes the resulting $w$ nonzero in $L$. Its lower-Levi commutators vanish in $L$: a potentially nonzero split has $l+1\in C$ and demands $B_{i,l}\cup B_{l+1,N}$. If its first factor survives, step 4.1 gives $|B_{i,l}|\le|C\cap(i,l)|$; since $|B_{i,N}|=|C|$ and $l+1\in C$, the suffix demands outnumber suffix supports, forcing the second factor into the radical. Higher divided generators have absent target weights. Thus $w$ is primitive. [F1] gives one-dimensionality and excludes every other primitive highest label. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $v_i$ be the nonzero primitive line for a matched removable row $i$ and $\Psi_i$ its cyclic lower-Schur module. If it has a proper nonzero submodule, that submodule contains a simple submodule, whose highest line is $v_h$ by [F1] and step 5.1. Triangular spanning puts its weight strictly below $\lambda(i)$, so $h<i$; equality would contain the generating line. The universal Weyl map onto $\Psi_i$ and [F2] force $\lambda(h)$ and $\lambda(i)$ to have the same residue multiset, hence $c_{h,i}=0$. Conversely suppose $h<i$ are matched and $c_{h,i}=0$. The demand/support sets split as $B_{h,N}=B_{h,i}\cup B_{i,N}$ and $C_{h,N}=C_{h,i}\cup\{i\}\cup C_{i,N}$. A prefix matching exists by restricting any matching for $h$ to demands below $i$; these cannot use later supports. Combine it with a matching for $i$, giving an image $C$ omitting $i$ with exactly $|B_{h,i}|$ earlier and $|B_{i,N}|$ later supports. Let $A=(h,N)\setminus C$, $k=\max(\{h\}\cup(C\cap(h,i)))$. Then $c_{k,i}=0$, and the recurrence at $i$ gives $$S_{h,N}(A)z=\mathbf1_{k\ne h}S_{h,N}((A\setminus\{i\})\cup\{k\})z+S_{h,i}(A\cap(h,i))S_{i,N}(A\cap(i,N))z.$$ When present, the first term replaces support $k<i$ by $i$; its earlier demands now outnumber earlier supports, so step 4.1 kills it in $L$. The other full and suffix vectors are the nonzero primitive vectors of step 5.1. Hence $v_h$ lies in $\Psi_i$ and generates a proper submodule. Thus $\Psi_i$ is simple precisely for the first matched row of its residue, and the full first-level socle is the multiplicity-free sum of these simples. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 2.2, algebra]

7.1 The matching criterion is exactly the signature criterion. A zero $c_{i,k}$ records a later removable push of the same residue and a zero $b_{i,k}$ a later addable pop; nonremovable equal rows have both slots and cancel as a neutral pair. Removing common demand/support slots preserves the prefix inequalities for $B\downarrow C$. The remaining prefix inequalities say that the minus at row $i$ survives all later pops. Thus matched rows are normal, and the first matched row of a residue is its good row. Good deletion preserves restrictedness: its only possible new gap $e$ is above the deleted row, when $\lambda_{i-1}-\lambda_i=e-1$. The adjacent removable corners then have the same residue and no intervening same-residue boundary corner; if the lower minus survives, the upper minus survives too, contradicting first-surviving selection. The dual adjacent-plus argument proves cogood addition preserves restrictedness. Flipping the selected minus to plus changes no other $i$-boundary status, since all other changed corners have residues $i\pm1$, different from $i$ even at $e=2$. Before the first surviving minus the stack is empty, and every suffix prefix has at least as many remaining minus pushes as plus pops; after the flip these are exactly the conditions for the last surviving plus. Hence good deletion and cogood addition are inverse partial moves on restricted partitions. [step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Transfer the socle through the actual corner, using more than exactness. By steps 6.1 and 7.1 all Schur socle labels of $V=L_N(\lambda)^1$ are restricted; [F3] makes their lower corners nonzero simples. Therefore $V$ has no nonzero corner-killed submodule, since every nonzero finite-dimensional submodule contains a simple submodule. For a simple lower-Hecke injection $D\hookrightarrow e_{\rm lower}V$, the corner adjunction gives $Ae_{\rm lower}\otimes_{e_{\rm lower}Ae_{\rm lower}}D\to V$, whose image $I$ is generated by $D$ and satisfies $e_{\rm lower}I=D$. A proper nonzero submodule $J<I$ has corner zero or $D$. The first contradicts the no-killed-submodule property; the second contains $D$ and thus generates $I$. Hence $I$ is simple. Conversely every surviving Schur socle simple has simple corner by [F3]. These inclusions prove $\operatorname{soc}_H(e_{\rm lower}V)=e_{\rm lower}\operatorname{soc}_A(V)$, with multiplicities and actual labels. [F1]'s explicit corner identifies this with the actual Hecke restriction of $D(\lambda)$. [F1, F3, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Define the primary functors over $F$. By [F3] the spectra of $L_d$ in the regular module are q-contents, hence among the distinct $[i]_q$, $i\in\mathbb Z/e$; cellular layers and their common triangular flags give this for the regular action as well. The polynomial CRT applied to $\prod_i(X-[i]_q)^{d!}$ gives mutually orthogonal projectors $P_{d,i}$, with sum one, in $F[L_d]$. They centralize $H_{d-1}$ and are star-fixed. Taking exponent $d!$ is sufficient for every Jordan block of the regular action and therefore every module; absent eigenvalues give the zero projector. On a good lower simple $D(\lambda\setminus A)$ in restriction, $L_d=\sum_{r\le d}L_r-\sum_{r<d}L_r$ has scalar $[c(A)]_q$: the symmetric sums have their actual cell scalars by [F2]. Thus its primary projector selects exactly the good residue. Every nonzero primary summand contains a simple socle submodule, so a summand with no good residue is zero. The form quotient makes $D(\lambda)$ star self-dual, and its star-fixed projector inherits a nondegenerate restricted form; its head is dual to its simple socle and has the same label. This proves the restriction endpoints when $q\ne1$. At $q=1$ use the actual group endpoint [F4], with the same primary construction and residue normalization. [F2, F3, F4, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Induction and restriction are biadjoint over $F$. Let $B=H_{d+1}$, $H=H_d$, and let $E_H:B\to H$ retain precisely the lower standard-basis terms. It is an $H$-bimodule map. For distinguished parabolic cosets $c,t$, the perfect trace gives $E_H(T_c^*T_t)=\delta_{c,t}q^{\ell(t)}$: pair against each lower basis element using $\tau_B(hE_H(a))=\tau_B(ha)$ and the disjoint length-additive coset supports. All diagonal values are units. Hence the relative Frobenius pairing gives $B\otimes_HX\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(B,X)$ naturally. For a commuting primary projector $p=P_{d+1,i}$, cyclicity of the trace and commutation with $H$ give $E_H(pa)=E_H(ap)$, by pairing both expressions against the lower algebra's perfect trace. Under this identification right multiplication by $p$ corresponds to selecting $p$ on restriction. Ordinary tensor adjunction and this Frobenius adjunction therefore give both $\operatorname{Hom}_B(F_iX,Y)=\operatorname{Hom}_H(X,E_iY)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_B(Y,F_iX)=\operatorname{Hom}_H(E_iY,X)$. [F3, step 9.1, algebra, construct]

11.1 For every simple label $\eta$ of rank $d+1$, step 9.1 and absolute simplicity give each of these Hom dimensions with $X=D(\mu)$, $Y=D(\eta)$ as one exactly when the good $i$-deletion of $\eta$ is $\mu$, and zero otherwise. Step 7.1 makes its inverse exactly the cogood addition, unique when defined. The complete cellular classifier [F3] covers every simple, so these two Hom tests identify respectively the simple head and simple socle of $F_iD(\mu)$, once each. If no cogood addition exists both tests vanish for every simple, forcing $F_iD(\mu)=0$ by finite dimensionality. At rank zero $H_0=H_1=F$, $L_1=0$, and the only move adds the residue-zero node; these formulas give $F_0F=F$ and every other summand zero. [F3, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, algebra]

12.1 Descend the temporary square-root extension. The Hecke modules, their cell forms, all primary projectors and functors above are defined over $F$. The cellular quotients of [F3] remain absolutely simple under $F\to K$, and finite-dimensional Hom spaces are kernels of finite linear systems over $F$, so their dimensions are unchanged by this field extension. Step 9.1's restriction and step 11.1's induction Hom tests therefore hold over $F$ itself and give exactly the stated endpoints. This argument also permits a purely inseparable square-root extension in characteristic two; no Galois averaging is used. The polynomial, integral module, actual corner and coefficient-functional constructions never divide a specialized Gram determinant. No primality condition on $e$ or Fock-space label classification entered the proof; no Choice principle is used. [F1, F3, step 9.1, step 11.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Jonathan Brundan, Modular branching rules and the Mullineux map for Hecke algebras of type A, §§4.2–5.7

rows.title: General Hecke cellular simple labels match the basic crystal
rows.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice only for the canonical basic-component identification through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]. The finite recursive cellular comparison adds no use of Choice.

Let $F$ be any field, $q\in F^\times$ of finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, and use the Murphy restricted labels $D(\lambda)$ and residue functors $E_i,F_i$ of [[lem-general-hecke-residue-branching-endpoints-from-normalized-schur-cells]], with residue $c-r\bmod e$. Recursively set $\dot D(\varnothing)=F$ and $\dot D(\lambda)=\operatorname{hd}F_i\dot D(\widetilde e_i\lambda)$ for any defined good deletion. This is defined at every restricted partition, independent of the selected deletion, and $\dot D(\lambda)\cong D(\lambda)$. This finite recursive comparison holds without Choice; only the canonical basic-component identification below assumes Choice. The finite recursive comparison adds no Choice use and does not use Fock-space classification to identify a module head. These restricted labels, with the displayed good/cogood operators, are the transported basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with weight $\Lambda_0-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The basic-component assertion carries the declared Choice in the integrable crystal decomposition of [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]. The assertion is for level-one type-A Hecke algebras; it supplies no arbitrary-level cyclotomic label theorem.
rows.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, finite quantum characteristic, exact cellular labels and residue functors of the Statement.

[F1] The proved general-Hecke endpoint supplies complete distinct absolutely simple restricted labels and $\operatorname{hd}F_iD(\mu)=D(\widetilde f_i\mu)$ when its cogood addition exists ([[lem-general-hecke-residue-branching-endpoints-from-normalized-schur-cells]]).

[F2] The actual full Fock crystal has canonical empty component $B(\Lambda_0)$, with the stated integrable-decomposition Choice ([[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]). Conjugation and color reflection carry its operators onto the restricted good-node graph and transport its weight as $\Lambda_0-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$ ([[prop-qg-fock-crystal-arrows-agree-with-the-modular-good-node-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 For a partition $\lambda$, list addable pluses and removable minuses of residue $i$ from top to bottom and cancel $-+$ pairs by a last-in-first-out minus stack. Deleting the first surviving minus and adding the last surviving plus are inverse selected moves. Indeed changing the selected corner changes its sign; every other altered boundary corner has residue $i+1$ or $i-1$, different from $i$ even at $e=2$. Immediately before a first surviving minus the minus stack is empty, and every suffix prefix has at least as many remaining minus pushes as plus pops. After flipping that minus to plus, these conditions say precisely that this plus survives and no later plus does. Reversing the flip proves the converse. This retains the positions of the selected signs, not just their counts. [given, algebra]

2.1 Good deletion preserves restrictedness. For a removable row $r$, only its gap and the gap immediately above can change: the former decreases by one and the latter increases by one. The only possible violation is $r>1$ and $\lambda_{r-1}-\lambda_r=e-1$. Then the removable corners in rows $r-1,r$ have equal residues, and their minus signs are adjacent in that residue word: the addable corners between them have residues differing by one. If the lower minus survives, the upper one also survives, since stack pops remove the lower minus first. The lower one therefore cannot be the first surviving minus. Cogood addition preserves restrictedness by the dual adjacent-plus argument: if its row gap were $e-1$, the later same-residue addable corner would survive whenever the earlier one did, contradicting selection of the last surviving plus. Hence step 1.1 gives inverse partial operations on the restricted vertex set. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every nonempty restricted partition has a good deletion. Let $h$ be its height. Its bottom removable node has residue $\lambda_h-h$, while the only boundary node below it is the addable $(h+1,1)$ of residue $-h$. The difference $\lambda_h$ lies strictly between zero and $e$, so these residues differ. There is consequently no later same-residue plus to cancel that bottom minus. At least one minus survives in that residue, and its first surviving minus is a good node. By step 2.1 its deletion stays restricted. Repeating decreases the number of boxes and ends at the empty diagram; reversing gives cogood additions by step 1.1. All selections may be made by the least residue and then the prescribed extremal sign, using finite sets. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Induct on rank to establish both definition and comparison simultaneously. At rank zero the two modules are $F$. Suppose comparison has been established for every smaller rank and let $\lambda$ be nonempty and restricted. Step 3.1 gives a defined predecessor, so the recursion has at least one option. For any allowed residue $i$, put $\mu=\widetilde e_i\lambda$. The induction hypothesis identifies the actual lower-rank module $\dot D(\mu)$ with $D(\mu)$; by steps 1.1 and 2.1 its cogood addition is $\widetilde f_i\mu=\lambda$. Thus [F1] identifies the recursively chosen head with the same simple module $D(\lambda)$ for every allowed $i$. This proves choice independence, existence and the displayed isomorphism at this rank and therefore at every rank. No comparison is used to prove the supplier's cellular endpoint, and no combinatorial connectedness alone identifies a module head. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F2] the restricted graph on these same shapes, with color $i$ and its prescribed good/cogood operations, is the transported canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$ and has the displayed weight. Step 4.1 identifies its recursively attached module at every vertex with the actual Murphy cellular simple. Thus the cellular and basic-crystal labels agree, while the endpoint producer itself used no crystal label comparison. The graph and finite recursive arguments add no Choice; the only inherited use is [F2]'s integrable crystal decomposition, as stated. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Jonathan Brundan, Modular branching rules and the Mullineux map for Hecke algebras of type A, §§2.1–2.11 and 5.3–5.7
Alexander Kleshchev, Representation theory of symmetric groups and related Hecke algebras, §11.2

rows.title: The crystal identification does not elementarily identify the cellular simple labels
rows.statement:
Two labellings of the simple modules of the group algebra $kS_d$ and of the
Hecke algebra $H_d$ are in play on this page and on the Fock-space page.

- The **cellular labels** $D(\mu)=\operatorname{hd}(S(\mu))$ are the heads of
  the Specht modules in the dual-Specht convention; they are the labels used
  by the modular classification
  ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
- The **inductive (crystal) labels** $\dot D(\mu)$ are defined recursively
  from the residue-summand functors $F_i$ of
  [[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] by
  $\dot D(\varnothing)=k$ and, for $\mu\ne\varnothing$,
$$\dot D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(F_i\dot D(\tilde e_i\mu)\bigr) \quad\text{for any }i\text{ for which }\tilde e_i\mu\text{ is defined},$$ the
  operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ being those of
  [[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]] and the independence
  of the choice of $i$ a theorem of the crystal theory. The two labellings
  agree, $$\dot D(\mu)\cong D(\mu)\qquad(\mu\ \text{p-restricted}),$$ and this
  identification (11.1) of Kleshchev's survey is *not* elementary: it was
  first established by Ariki and later by graded arguments, both depending on
  the full theory of the cyclotomic Hecke/KLR categorification.

Consequently no proof on this page or on the later Fock-space page may use
Fock-space reachability to establish the cellular classification of simple
modules, or the cellular classification to establish the Fock-space
component; the two directions are separated by this reminder. In particular
the socle theorem
`cor-socle-of-uncoloured-modular-restriction-is-the-sum-over-good-residues`
and the branching theorems of this page are stated and used for the cellular
labels, while any statement about the crystal operators as operators on Fock
space is a separate obligation of the Fock-space page.
rows.strategy:
## Remarks

- **Why the identification is not formal.** The definition of $\dot D(\mu)$
  uses only the functors $F_i$ and the already-constructed simple modules of
  smaller rank, whereas $D(\mu)$ is the head of an explicit Specht module;
  the equality of the two families is a strong statement about the
  categorification, not a consequence of the combinatorial inverse property
  of the operators.
- **The direction used here.** Only the cellular labels are assigned
  module-theoretic meaning on this page; the symbol $\dot D(\mu)$ occurs on
  the Fock-space page, where the identification is available through the
  cited theorem.

The actual level-one construction now supplies the required module-theoretic comparison over every field and invertible parameter of finite quantum characteristic, including composite quantum characteristic: [[lem-general-hecke-residue-branching-endpoints-from-normalized-schur-cells]] constructs the cellular restriction and induction endpoints through the normalized quantum Schur cells, polynomial lowering operators and actual regular corner.

Here is the finite comparison independently of any later Fock-space item. Every nonempty restricted shape has a good deletion: its bottom removable corner has residue $\lambda_h-h$, whereas the only boundary corner below it is the addable $(h+1,1)$ of residue $-h$; since $0<\lambda_h<e$, that bottom minus cannot be canceled. A first surviving minus therefore exists, and the endpoint supplier's finite signature argument proves its deletion remains restricted and its inverse is the prescribed cogood addition. Induct on rank. At rank zero both attached modules are $F$. At a larger rank every allowed predecessor $\nu=\widetilde e_i\lambda$ already has inductive module $D(\nu)$ by induction. Its actual cogood induction head, proved in the cellular endpoint supplier, is $D(\widetilde f_i\nu)=D(\lambda)$. Thus every allowed deletion gives the same actual cellular module, and the bottom-row argument ensures there is an option. This proof uses no Fock classification or Choice.

This is the local level-one route; the non-elementary history in the Statement concerns the broader cyclotomic labelling theorem and does not preclude this constructive rank induction. The later [[lem-general-hecke-cellular-simple-labels-match-the-basic-crystal]] additionally identifies the graph with canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$ through the independent Fock-component suppliers and carries their declared Axiom of Choice. That later canonical crystal clause is not a premise of the cellular endpoint or of the finite recursive comparison just proved here. The group-specialization functors retain the normalization of [[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]; the general Hecke primary projectors are constructed directly in the endpoint supplier.

references.title: Alexander Kleshchev, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups and Related Hecke Algebras, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 47 (2010) 419-481, author arXiv version; §11.2 with the inductive definition of D-dot(mu) as the head of F_i D-dot(e-tilde_i mu) and the labelling conjecture (11.1), printed pp. 51-52, and §11.2 for the references to S. Ariki's proof and the graded argument [40, Theorems 5.13, 5.18]. Complete 66-page text, SHA-256 8685199608967fa7c479e4dd883990b716a6f708e71cf75f6ce4aba41c6f2cab

rows.title: Normal and good nodes for the partition (6,4,4,3,2)
rows.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^\times$, and use the Hecke algebra
$H(r)$ with $(T_j-q)(T_j+1)=0$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
Here $\ell=e(F,q)$ is its quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), taken
in turn to be $3$ or $4$. The case $\ell=4$ means a parameter of order $4$
and is not a field of characteristic $4$; both cases occur over $F=\mathbb C$
with $q$ a primitive root of the specified order. Use Brundan's restricted
DJ labels: $S^\lambda$ here denotes the ordinary right Specht module
labelled by $\lambda'$ and $D^\lambda$ its simple head, as in his §2.1.
Right modules may be carried to left modules through the Hecke
anti-involution fixing the generators; this preserves socles and direct
sum decompositions. These source labels must not be silently identified
with the same-shape Murphy labels of the group-theoretic suppliers.

Work Brundan's Example 2.8 (complete 34-page author manuscript, p. 5) in his
conventions: $\lambda=(6,4,4,3,2)$, padded by $\lambda_6=0$ with $n=6$, is $\ell$-restricted for $\ell=3$ and
$\ell=4$, residues are $r-c\bmod\ell$ in the source's orientation (the
negative of the $c-r$ convention of this page,
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]),
$R(\lambda)=\{1,3,4,5\}$ is the set of removable rows, and for
$i\in R(\lambda)$ one compares $B_{i,6}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ with
$C_{i,6}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ in the lattice order $\downarrow$, where
$$B_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in[i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k+1,\lambda_{k+1}+1)\},\qquad C_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in(i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k,\lambda_k)\},$$
and $A\downarrow B$ means that there is an injection $\theta:A\to B$ with
$\theta(a)\le a$ for all $a$.

For $\ell=3$ the removable nodes have residues $1,2,1,0$ for
$i=1,3,4,5$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{4\}),\ (\{4,5\},\varnothing), (\varnothing,\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,4,5\}$ and, since rows $4$ and $1$ share
residue $1$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1,5\}$. For $\ell=4$ the residues are
$3,3,1,3$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{3,5\}),\ (\varnothing,\{5\}), (\{5\},\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence row $4$ is normal-refuted by $\{5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$ and
$R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,3,5\}$, and since rows $1,3,5$ share residue $3$,
$R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1\}$. By the branching theorems the restriction of
$D^{\lambda}$ to $H(r-1)$ is therefore decomposable for $\ell=3$ (socle
$D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}\oplus D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$) and indecomposable for $\ell=4$
(socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}$).
rows.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The partition $\lambda=(6,4,4,3,2)$ of $r=19$, the field and invertible Hecke parameters with quantum characteristics $\ell=3$ and $\ell=4$, and Brundan's index sets and lattice order as displayed.

[F1] The source's definitions: $R(\lambda)=\{i:\lambda_i\ne\lambda_{i+1}\}$ is the set of removable rows, the node $(i,\lambda_i)$ has residue $i-\lambda_i\bmod\ell$, $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{i\in R(\lambda):B_{i,n}(\lambda)\downarrow C_{i,n}(\lambda)\}$ with $n=6$, and $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{i\in R^{normal}(\lambda):$ no $j\in R^{normal}(\lambda)$ with $j<i$ and the same residue$\}$; there is at most one good row per residue (Brundan §2.2-2.4 and Remark 2.7, printed pp. 3-5). The translation to this page's conventions is the transposed-node dictionary of Remark 2.4(II) ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]).

[F2] The actual general-Hecke endpoint [[lem-general-hecke-residue-branching-endpoints-from-normalized-schur-cells]] gives the multiplicity-free good-deletion socle for Murphy restricted labels. Brundan's source-labelled simple here is $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{source}}\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$, where $\theta(T_j)=q-1-T_j$: this is the actual unit-scaled ordinary module/form dictionary applied at ordinary shape $\lambda'$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). The automorphism respects the tower, so twisting both sides transfers the socle and all direct-sum conclusions without renaming a Murphy simple as an untwisted source simple. Distinct good-deletion source simples are separated by the central operator $\theta(\sum_{a=1}^{r-1}L_a)$: on $D_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ its scalar is the actual Murphy scalar $\sum_{A\in[\mu]}[c(A)]_q$ of [[lem-q-schur-central-hecke-jm-scalars-give-residue-separation]]. For two deletions of different residues their scalar difference is the difference of their distinct q-contents, hence nonzero. Polynomial primary projectors in this central operator separate the full restricted module, not merely its socle. This proves the required separation without a sufficient same-content block-classification premise.

[F3] A nonzero finite-dimensional module has nonzero socle: choose a nonzero submodule of least positive dimension. Thus a module with simple socle is indecomposable, because the socle of a direct sum is the direct sum of the summand socles ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). No self-duality of cell modules is assumed.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Removable rows and residues. $\lambda=(6,4,4,3,2)$ has consecutive differences $2,0,1,1,2$, so $R(\lambda)=\{1,3,4,5\}$ and $\lambda$ is $\ell$-restricted for $\ell=3$ and $\ell=4$; the residues $i-\lambda_i$ are, modulo $3$, $1,2,1,0$ for $i=1,3,4,5$, and modulo $4$, $3,3,1,3$ for the same rows. [given, F1]

2.1 Pad by $\lambda_6=0$. For $k=1,\ldots,5$, the integers $k-\lambda_{k+1}$ are $(-3,-2,0,2,5)$ and $k-\lambda_k$ are $(-5,-2,-1,1,3)$. To compute $B_{i,6}$ use indices $i\le k<6$ with the first integer congruent to $i-\lambda_i$; for $C_{i,6}$ use $i<k<6$ with the second integer congruent to $i-\lambda_i$, then intersect with $R=\{1,3,4,5\}$. For $i=1,3,4,5$, respectively, this gives $(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{4\}),(\{4,5\},\varnothing),(\varnothing,\varnothing),(\varnothing,\varnothing)$ modulo $3$, and $(\varnothing,\{3,5\}),(\varnothing,\{5\}),(\{5\},\varnothing),(\varnothing,\varnothing)$ modulo $4$. These are exactly the corrected displayed pairs. [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 For $\ell=3$, rows $1,4,5$ pass the lattice test: their demand sets are empty. Row $3$ fails because $\{4,5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$. Hence $R^{normal}=\{1,4,5\}$, with residues $1,1,0$; taking the least normal row in each residue gives $R^{good}=\{1,5\}$. For $\ell=4$, rows $1,3,5$ pass, while row $4$ fails because $\{5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$. The normal rows all have residue $3$, so $R^{good}=\{1\}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1]

4.1 $\ell=3$: decomposability.
